entry: Early Christian bishop of Myra in [[Anatolia]] and patron saint of sailors, merchants, children and students. Little is known of his historical life, and the earliest accounts were written centuries after his death. Legend credits him with rescuing three girls from forced prostitution by dropping a sack of gold coins through their window, and with calming a storm at sea. An early list places him at the [[First Council of Nicaea]] in 325, but no contemporary writing confirms it. Radiocarbon dating of a relic fragment supports a fourth-century origin for his cult. In 1087 merchants from [[Bari]], Italy, removed most of his bones to their city, and Venetian sailors later took remaining fragments to [[Venice]] during the [[First Crusade]]. His secret gift-giving gave rise to the folklore of [[Santa Claus]].

Capital city of [[Minnesota]], United States (pop., 2020: 311,527), on a bend of the [[Mississippi River]] neighboring [[Minneapolis]]. Together they form the core of the Twin Cities metropolitan area, the third most populous in the Midwest. The Minnesota State Capitol stands on a hill above downtown. The town was established as capital of the Minnesota Territory in 1849, and in the 19th century it became headquarters of James J. Hill's railroad empire. It is the county seat of Ramsey County.

Apostle of [[Jesus]] and one of the first leaders of the early Christian Church. Born Simon bar Jonah, he was a fisherman and the brother of Andrew. Jesus gave him the Aramaic name Cephas, meaning rock or stone, and he appears prominently in all four New Testament gospels and in the Acts of the Apostles. Catholic and Orthodox tradition treats him as the first bishop of [[Rome]] and of [[Antioch]]. According to Christian tradition, he was crucified upside down in Rome under [[Nero]]. Early Church Fathers, including [[Irenaeus]] and [[Tertullian]], attest that he spent his last years in Rome, although the New Testament does not say so. Modern scholarship generally rejects Petrine authorship of the two New Testament letters attributed to him.

Second-largest city in [[Russia]] (pop., 2021: 5,601,911), on the [[Neva]] River at the head of the Gulf of Finland. Founded by [[Peter the Great]] on May 27, 1703, on the site of a captured Swedish fortress, it was named after the apostle Saint Peter. It was the capital of the [[Russian Empire]] from 1712 to 1918, except c. 1728–1730, but after the [[October Revolution]] the Bolsheviks moved the government to [[Moscow]]. Renamed Leningrad in 1924, the city endured the [[Siege of Leningrad]] during World War II. Its original name was restored in 1991. It is home to the Hermitage, one of the largest art museums in the world, and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Self-governing overseas collectivity of [[France]] (pop., 2026 est.: 5,513), an archipelago of eight islands in the northwestern [[Atlantic Ocean]] off Canada's [[Newfoundland (island)|Newfoundland]]. Residents are French citizens who elect a deputy to the National Assembly. It is an overseas country and territory of the [[European Union]] that uses the euro but lies outside the [[Schengen Area|Schengen area]]. Services, including public administration, make up over 80 percent of GDP. Its traditional fishing economy has declined through depleted stocks and maritime boundary disputes with Canada. The capital, Saint-Pierre, is French for Saint Peter, patron saint of fishermen.

Killing of seven members and associates of [[Chicago]]'s North Side Gang on Saint Valentine's Day 1929. Gunmen, some disguised as police, lined the men against a wall and shot them with Thompson submachine guns and a shotgun. The killings came amid Prohibition-era competition for control of [[Organized crime|organized crime]]. Police speculated that the gang's leader, George Moran, was the target, but he had not arrived. Suspicion fell on [[Al Capone]], head of the rival [[Chicago Outfit]], but no one was convicted. Violence with Thompson guns, including this massacre, led to gun control law, including the National Firearms Act of 1934.

Archipelagic country in the eastern [[Caribbean]], made up of the island of Saint Vincent and the northern two-thirds of the Grenadines. [[Christopher Columbus]] named the main island after St. Vincent of Saragossa. Most residents descend from enslaved Africans brought by France and later Britain, which contested the islands in the 18th century. The country was a British colony from 1783 until independence in 1979. Before European arrival the Kalinago called the island Youloumain. It remains a [[Commonwealth of Nations|Commonwealth]] realm, with [[Charles III]] as head of state, and is a member of CARICOM. In April 2021 the La Soufrière volcano erupted, forcing the evacuation of 16,000 residents.

Largest island and capital of the [[Northern Mariana Islands]], an unincorporated territory of the [[United States]] in the western [[Pacific Ocean]] (pop., 2020 est.: 43,385). Spanish rule from the 17th century ended with the [[Spanish–American War]] in 1898, and the island was then sold to Germany. [[Japan]] ruled it for 30 years, until the Battle of Saipan in [[World War II]]. Afterward it was administered by the United States within the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. In 1978 Saipan became part of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands. Today it holds about 90 percent of the territory's population.

Republic of [[Russia]], with about one million residents, and the largest subnational division in the world, covering 3,083,523 square kilometers (1,190,555 sq mi) of northeastern [[Siberia]]. Its capital, [[Yakutsk]], is the world's coldest major city, where winter averages commonly dip below −35 °C (−31 °F). The Turkic Sakha people, who came from the area of [[Lake Baikal]], reached the middle [[Lena River]] valley between the 9th and 16th centuries. Russians incorporated the region into the [[Tsardom of Russia]] in the 17th century and collected fur tribute from its peoples. Soviet-era migration brought many Russians and Ukrainians to the republic. It became the Republic of Sakha (Yakutia) in 1991, and it produces most of Russia's diamonds.

Island in northeastern Asia, part of [[Russia]] and the largest island in the country, with an area of 72,492 square kilometers. It separates the [[Sea of Okhotsk]] from the [[Sea of Japan]]. Its name derives from the Manchu word Sahaliyan, meaning black. China, Russia and Japan all claimed the island at different times, and the [[Ainu people|Ainu]] paid tribute to Chinese dynasties. In 1875 Japan ceded its claims to Russia in exchange for the northern [[Kuril Islands]]. After the [[Russo-Japanese War]], the island was divided in 1905, with the south going to Japan. Japan ruled the whole island from 1918 to 1925. Russia seized the Japanese portion in 1945 and has held all of the island since. Most Ainu moved to [[Hokkaido]] in 1949.

headword: Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom
sort_key: salo or the 120 days of sodom
entry: 1975 political art horror film by [[Pier Paolo Pasolini]], his last, released three weeks after his murder. It loosely adapts the [[Marquis de Sade|Marquis de Sade's]] novel *The 120 Days of Sodom*, moving the story to the fascist Italian Social Republic during [[World War II]]. Four wealthy libertines kidnap teenagers and subject them to extreme violence. The four segments are inspired by Dante's *Divine Comedy*, and the film explores political corruption, consumerism, authoritarianism and fascism. It premiered in Paris in 1975, was banned in Italy in 1976, and remains banned in many countries.

Dish of mixed ingredients, frequently [[Vegetable|vegetables]], usually served chilled or at room temperature and often with a dressing. Garden salads are made from leafy greens such as [[Lettuce|lettuce]], spinach or kale, often with tomato and [[Cucumber|cucumber]]. Other types include bean, potato, pasta and fruit salads, and dessert salads made with gelatin or whipped cream. Salad dressings are usually based on oil and vinegar or a creamy dairy base. The word comes from Latin salata, meaning salted, because Romans seasoned vegetables with [[Brine|brine]]. Ancient Greeks and Romans ate mixed greens with dressing. The [[Caesar salad]] was devised by Italian immigrant Caesar Cardini in Tijuana, Mexico, in 1924, and the salad bar first appeared in [[American English]] in 1937.

Sunni Muslim ruler of Kurdish origin who founded the Ayyubid dynasty and became the first sultan of Egypt and Syria. Sent to [[Fatimid Caliphate|Fatimid]] Egypt in 1164 with his uncle Shirkuh, he became vizier to the Fatimid caliph al-Adid. In 1171 he abolished the Fatimid Caliphate, an Isma'ili dynasty, and realigned Egypt with the Sunni [[Abbasid Caliphate]]. After the death of Nur ad-Din he conquered Syria, including [[Damascus]], and by 1182 had taken [[Aleppo]]. At the Battle of Hattin in 1187 his army defeated the [[Crusader states|Crusaders]] and captured [[Jerusalem]]. His reconquest provoked the [[Third Crusade]], in which he faced [[Richard I of England]]; the Treaty of Jaffa preserved Muslim sovereignty over Jerusalem. He died in Damascus after giving away much of his personal wealth to his subjects.

Order of [[Amphibian|amphibians]] (Urodela) with lizard-like bodies, blunt snouts, short limbs and a tail in both larval and adult stages. More than 740 species are known. Diversity is highest in eastern [[North America]], especially in the [[Appalachian Mountains]]. Their permeable skin keeps most species reliant on moist habitats, and some are fully aquatic while others are terrestrial as adults. Many lay eggs in water, though life cycles vary widely. Salamanders can regenerate limbs, tails and parts of the heart, jaw and spinal cord without scarring, making them a widespread [[Model organism|model organism]] in regeneration research. The Chinese giant salamander can reach 1.8 m (6 ft).

Series of hearings and prosecutions of people accused of [[Witchcraft|witchcraft]] in colonial Massachusetts from February 1692 to May 1693. More than 200 people were accused and 30 convicted; nineteen were [[Hanging|hanged]], and Giles Corey died under torture for refusing to enter a plea. At least five others died in jail without trial. It was the deadliest witch hunt in colonial North America. Clergymen's doubts about spectral evidence ended the trials. In 1702 the General Court declared them unlawful, and in 1711 the colonial legislature annulled the convictions. The last convicted Salem witch was officially exonerated in 2022.

Commercial exchange in which a seller transfers ownership of goods or services to a buyer for money or other agreed consideration. The term can also denote the quantity or value of goods sold in a period, or a period of reduced prices. The seller typically executes the sale, which may be completed before payment. Its boundaries with [[Advertising]], [[Public relations]] and [[Marketing]] are often unclear, and from a management viewpoint sales is a part of marketing. Sales departments are often separate corporate groupings staffed by salespeople. In the United States, most states have adopted Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code, while other [[Common law|common law]] countries govern sales by the common law and commercial codes. A potential buyer is called a prospect.

Tax paid to a [[Government|government]] on the sale of certain goods and services, usually collected by the seller from the consumer at the point of purchase. A use tax is paid directly by the consumer on goods bought without sales tax, such as from a vendor in another state. Laws often exempt food, education and medicines. A [[Value-added tax|value-added tax]] (VAT) applies at each stage of sale to the value added, which avoids the cascading of taxes. Most countries levy sales or value-added taxes. [[Norway]], [[Denmark]] and [[Sweden]] have VATs of 25 percent, and [[Hungary]] has the highest rate, at 27 percent. Over 140 countries have VAT systems, leaving the United States as one of few nations that use a conventional sales tax; 45 states impose statewide sales taxes.

Organic compound (C₇H₆O₃), a colorless, bitter-tasting solid and precursor to [[Aspirin|aspirin]]. Its name comes from Latin salix, for [[Willow|willow]] tree, from which it was first identified. It is a plant hormone and a metabolite of aspirin. In medicine it removes the outer layer of skin and treats [[Wart|warts]], [[Psoriasis]], [[Acne|acne]] and dandruff. It is also a food preservative. Bismuth subsalicylate, a salt of [[Bismuth|bismuth]] and salicylic acid, is an active ingredient in stomach-relief aids. The European Union restricts its concentration in cosmetics and bars its use in products for children under three, other than shampoos.

Indian screenwriter, actor and film producer, best known as half of the screenwriting duo Salim–Javed with Javed Akhtar. Salim mainly developed stories and characters, while Akhtar wrote dialogue and screenplays. Their 1970s films, including *Zanjeer* (1973), *Deewaar* (1975) and *Sholay* (1975), revolutionized Indian cinema and created the angry young man archetype embodied by [[Amitabh Bachchan]]. *Sholay* became the highest-grossing Indian film of its time. Khan has won six Filmfare Awards for the partnership's work. Born in [[Indore]] into an affluent family, he is the father of actor [[Salman Khan]].

American actress known for screen and stage roles. She won two [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]] for Best Actress, for *Norma Rae* (1979) and *Places in the Heart* (1984), and was nominated for playing Mary Todd Lincoln in *Lincoln* (2012). She rose to fame in the ABC sitcoms *Gidget* and *The Flying Nun*. She won four Primetime Emmy Awards, including for *Sybil* (1976), the medical drama [[ER (TV series)|ER]] and *Brothers & Sisters*. Her films include *Smokey and the Bandit*, *Steel Magnolias*, *Mrs. Doubtfire* and *Forrest Gump*. On Broadway she was nominated for a Tony Award for *The Glass Menagerie*.

Irish novelist, educated at Trinity College [[Dublin]]. Her novels include *Conversations with Friends* (2017), *Normal People* (2018) and *Intermezzo* (2024). *Normal People* won the Costa Book Award and the Irish Book Award in 2018, and the first two novels were adapted as television miniseries. Rooney has described herself as both a feminist and a Marxist. She is a prominent advocate of Palestinian liberation, including the group Palestine Action, which has led to her being banned in the United Kingdom from public speaking and from receiving royalties for her works. Critics have accused her of selective activism.

Mexican and American actress and film producer. She began her career in Mexico before establishing herself in Hollywood with *Desperado* (1995) and *From Dusk till Dawn* (1996). Her portrayal of [[Frida Kahlo]] in *Frida* (2002), which she also produced, earned an Academy Award nomination for Best Actress, the first for a Mexican actress. Her role as Ajak in the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]] film *Eternals* (2021) became her highest-grossing live-action film. Her work on the ABC comedy-drama *Ugly Betty* earned two Primetime Emmy nominations. [[Time (magazine)|Time magazine]] named her one of the 100 most influential people in the world in 2023.

Indian actor, film producer and television presenter working mainly in Hindi cinema. His breakthrough, *Maine Pyar Kiya* (1989), was followed by commercially successful action films such as *Dabangg* (2010) and *Tiger Zinda Hai* (2017). He has hosted the reality show *Bigg Boss* since 2010. In 2015 he was convicted of culpable homicide over a driving accident that killed one person, but the conviction was set aside on appeal. In 2018 he was convicted in a [[Blackbuck|blackbuck]] poaching case and sentenced to five years' imprisonment, but he was granted bail pending appeal. He is the son of [[Salim Khan]].

Indian-born British and American novelist whose work combines magical realism with historical fiction, often about relations between Eastern and Western civilizations. His second novel, *Midnight's Children* (1981), won the [[Booker Prize]]. *The Satanic Verses* (1988), which some saw as an irreverent depiction of [[Muhammad]], led to a fatwa calling for his death, issued by [[Ruhollah Khomeini]], and the book was banned in 20 countries. In 2022 he survived a stabbing at the Chautauqua Institution that cost him the sight of one eye. Educated at the [[University of Cambridge]], he was knighted in 2007 for services to literature. [[Time (magazine)|Time magazine]] named him one of the 100 most influential people in the world in 2023.

Saudi king, reigning since 2015, and a member of the [[House of Saud]]. He was governor of [[Riyadh]] for almost half a century, and was appointed defense minister in 2011 and crown prince in 2012. His major initiatives as king include Saudi Vision 2030, a 2017 decree allowing women to drive, and military intervention in the [[Yemeni civil war (2014–present)|Yemeni civil war]]. His son [[Mohammed bin Salman]], who replaced him as prime minister in 2022, is considered the de facto ruler.
